Name: Adam
Transcript: This is our last one. The season's over, more or less. Looking back over the year, what has it been like for you, keeping the plot?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Mixed. Very mixed. We had a harvest, a proper harvest, if you count sunflower seeds and about nine strawberries. Nine. We counted them. And courgettes, so many courgettes, from my mother's half. Courgettes every day, courgette soup, courgette cake, I gave courgettes to the whole street. The kids think we are farmers now. Matei tells everybody, we have a farm. And I think, we got away with it. That's how it feels. We got to the end of the year and nobody threw us out, and the children think it was wonderful. We got away with it.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You got away with it. What do you mean?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Like I didn't deserve it. Like an exam where you didn't study and somehow you pass. When I gave the courgettes to the neighbours, everybody said, oh, you grew these? Amazing. And I said yes. Yes, I grew them. And it's half a lie. My mother grew them. I picked them. So I felt a bit like a, how do you say, a fake. Smiling with my mother's courgettes. And the strawberries, nine strawberries, those were really ours. Those I'm proud of. Nine strawberries I can stand behind.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What was the harvest like for the children?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Oh, for them it was the best. Matei cut the sunflower heads himself, with Chris, with the big scissors. And he dried them on the windowsill, and he picked out every seed, one by one, a whole evening, and he put them in an envelope. And he wrote on it, Matei sunflowers next year. In his own writing, with the s backwards. It's on the fridge now. And Daria picked the strawberries. Seven of the nine she picked, and she ate four before we got home. Five. We argued about it. She says four.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And for you, how has the year been?

Name: Nell
Transcript: I'm giving up half. I decided in September. The committee lets you share a plot, so you keep half and somebody else takes half. A retired couple are taking the far end, Jean and Malcolm, very nice people, they were on the list for a long time. So I keep the half by the shed, with Matei's corner. I felt like I had failed. When I decided, I felt like I had failed. And then I felt relieved. Both. And I still don't know which one is right. Maybe both are right. Is possible.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Failed, and then relieved. Can you tell me about each?

Name: Nell
Transcript: The failing. I wrote the email to the secretary three times. Three times I wrote it and deleted it. Because I know what it means. It means the man with the hat was right. It means I took too much, again, like always, and I couldn't hold it. That's the failing. And then I sent it, and I went to bed, and the next morning I woke up and the first thought in my head was not the plot. First time since March. The first thought was, oh, it's raining. Just that. Oh, it's raining. And I felt, how to say, like when you take off a backpack you forgot you were carrying. That's the relief.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What did your mother say, when you told her?

Name: Nell
Transcript: I was afraid to tell her. I thought she would be disappointed, after all her work. Three weeks of her work, and I give it away. But she didn't say this. She said, good, Nell. She said, you have two small children, a plot is too much, I told you in March. I said, mama, in March you laughed. She said, yes, I laughed because it was too much. So she was not laughing at me. She was laughing at the too much. All year I thought she was laughing at me, at the village girl digging in England. And she was laughing at the too much. Is different. I didn't know it was different.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And Jean and Malcolm are taking the far end.

Name: Nell
Transcript: Yes. And this is the thing. The far end is my mother's half. The good half. The half that looked like my buni's. I gave away the good half and I kept the half with the jungle and Matei's sunflowers. Chris said, are you crazy, give them the jungle, keep the good half. But I said no. Because that half is ours. Me and the children. Mama's half was never mine. It was beautiful, but it was never mine. I was a guest there. I don't want to keep a half where I'm a guest.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Mama's half was never yours.

Name: Nell
Transcript: No. And I thought about this a lot, in the autumn. In March I told you I want the children to know where food comes from, like me at my buni's. And this is true, I want this. But I think also, I wanted to be at my buni's again. Not to have a garden. To be in her garden. To be nine years old with the bucket and the beans and her humming. And you cannot dig that. You can dig all day in England and you will not find it. Is not in the soil. I phoned her, my buni, in October. She's ninety-two now. I told her about the plot, the courgettes, the sunflowers. And she laughed and she asked me, and the tomatoes, Nell? How are the tomatoes? And I said, buni, I didn't plant tomatoes. And she laughed more. She was happy that I'm trying. That was enough. That was more than enough.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You didn't plant tomatoes.

Name: Nell
Transcript: No. The seeds came, in March, in a letter from my mother, from the village. Tomato seeds from my uncle's neighbour, wrapped in a bit of newspaper. And I never planted them. There was never the right day. First it was too cold, then I was too busy, then it was too late. They're still in the envelope, in the kitchen drawer. Buni's tomatoes, from the village, in a drawer in England. Maybe next year. Matei says he will plant them with his sunflowers. I think maybe he will. I think maybe they are his to plant, not mine.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What will the plot be next year?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Smaller. And the children's. I have stopped pretending it's my hobby. All year I told people, oh, my allotment, my allotment, like the English ladies with their hobby. But it was not a hobby. It was one more job, with a letter from a boss. I was pretending to be relaxed about it. Now I don't pretend. It's their place. Matei wants pumpkins next year, a giant pumpkin, he saw one on television. Daria wants, I don't know, she wants to water things. It's their place, and I'm glad they have one. Really glad. Every child should have a place like this.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Pretending to be relaxed about it.

Name: Nell
Transcript: Yes. Everybody here, the English people, they say, oh, I just potter, I just potter about. Potter. I learned this word this year. And I wanted to be a person who potters. Relaxed, with a cup of tea. But I don't potter. I attack. I go to the plot like I go to a war. And then I come home and somebody asks and I say, oh, I was just pottering. Is a lie. Is the biggest lie of my year, the pottering.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And your body, this autumn?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Better. My back is better, since I gave up half. Not because of the half, I think. Because I stopped running. In September, after I sent the email, I slept. A whole week I slept like the children. Chris said, are you ill? I said no, I'm just not behind any more. And the good tired came back, one time, in October, after we lifted the last potatoes from my half, the little ones. My arms ached, and it was the good ache. The warm one. I remember I told you about it, in March. It came back for one day.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Has anything about the year surprised you?

Name: Nell
Transcript: That I minded so much. I thought, it's just a plot, it's just some mud. But I walked past the far end last week, to get to the water tap, and Malcolm has already dug it over, and there were leeks. His leeks, in a row, very straight, where my mother's dill was. And I had a little moment. Just a little one. I stood there with the watering can. Is stupid. They're leeks.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What was the little moment like?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Like when you walk past your old flat, the one you lived in before, and you see somebody else's curtains in the window. You know this feeling? Is not your flat any more, you gave it back, it's fine, you have a better one now. But the curtains. Somebody else's curtains, where your life was. Like this. Malcolm's leeks where my mother's dill was, where my buni's garden was for three weeks. Is fine. It's only a little moment. And then I went to the tap.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Somebody else's curtains, where your life was. Do you know that feeling from other places?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Sometimes. When I go back to the village, every time, there is something. A new house where the old shop was. A neighbour who died. My school is a supermarket now. You go back and somebody else has their curtains in your life. That's what it is to leave, I think. Everything you left keeps going without you. Is normal. But the plot, I didn't expect it there, in England. I didn't think I would feel this about a half plot in England. That's what surprised me.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And the other plot holders, how are they for you now?

Name: Nell
Transcript: This surprised me also. They are kind. Really kind. Jean gave Matei a pumpkin from her old allotment, a big orange one, he carried it home like a baby. And the man with the hat, from March, the one who looked at my pushchair. He came in October and he gave Daria a strawberry plant in a pot. For the little gardener, he said. He knows her name now. So maybe they never thought I'm crazy. Maybe only I thought this. All year I felt them looking at me, and maybe they were just looking at the weather. I don't know. But the letter, the letter from the committee, I still have it. I don't know why I keep it. It's in the drawer with the passports.

Name: Adam
Transcript: In the drawer with the passports.

Name: Nell
Transcript: Yes. Is a strange place, I know. The important papers drawer. Birth certificates, passports, my qualification, the letter that says you can stay. And this one. Your plot is not being cultivated to the required standard. I don't know why I put it there. Maybe because it's important, in a bad way. A paper that says something about me. Maybe I will throw it away next year. Maybe not. Chris laughed when he saw it there. I didn't laugh.

Name: Adam
Transcript: In March you wanted one thing that was yours. How is that now?

Name: Nell
Transcript: One Sunday in October, Chris took the kids swimming, and I went to the plot alone. And I opened the deckchair. First time. The striped one. It was a bit mouldy from the shed. And I sat in it, with the book, in the sun, it was a warm day for October. Exactly the picture I had in March. And I sat for ten minutes. Then I got up and I started weeding. I couldn't stay. I don't know how to sit. I think here I learned to always be doing, always, and I forgot how to sit. My buni can sit. My buni sits for hours. I sat for ten minutes. But ten minutes is not nothing. Maybe next year twenty.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Ten minutes is not nothing.

Name: Nell
Transcript: No. For me it's big. Ten minutes in a chair with nobody needing me, nobody behind me, no phone. I didn't read the book. I opened it, I didn't read. I just looked at Matei's sunflowers, the dead ones, brown, with their heads down. And I thought, they did their job. They're finished. They can stand there with their heads down and nobody shouts at them. And then I got up and weeded, of course. But for ten minutes I was like the sunflowers.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Is there anything else, about the year, that I haven't asked about?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Only that I think I'm less strict. With me, I mean. A little bit. In March I had the calendar, two mornings, minimum, and I was so strict, and I did it four times. And I was so angry with myself. Now I think, okay. Four times. It was a hard year. My buni, when I told her about the calendar, she said, the garden doesn't care if you're strict, Nell. The garden doesn't read your calendar. And I laughed, but she's right. I think I am learning a little bit of slow. Very little. But a little.
